description: We are a multidisciplinary team bridging the worlds of interactive web development and immersive digital storytelling. Our mission is to take complex Earth and space science concepts and transform them into engaging, accessible, and narrative driven web experiences that anyone can explore and connect with.
summary: Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a free 3D browser game that tells the story of NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. Players act as researchers: they launch from Earth, land on the Moon and Mars, and find 25 real artifacts, including the Surveyor landers, Apollo descent stages and rovers, Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity. Each artifact opens a card with its mission year, purpose, fate, coordinates and links to the official NASA source. Back on Earth, players submit a mission report and answer quiz questions about what they collected, so they have to read the facts to pass. It addresses the challenge by turning storytelling into play for students and space fans. It matters because these missions are easy to forget once the headlines fade, and this lets people discover them one by one.
details:
What it does: Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a first-person 3D exploration game. The player starts at an Earth launch base, enters a rocket, launches into space, and chooses the Moon or Mars. On each world, tall beacons mark real NASA artifacts. Walking up to one and interacting opens a data card with the mission year, what it did, why it was left behind, its coordinates and links to the official NASA source. Oxygen drains away from the rocket, so players return to refill. After collecting, players return to Earth, enter how many items they collected and answer quiz questions drawn from those items. A full pass needs all 25 artifacts.

How it works: All facts are stored in two JSON files (moon.json with 17 artifacts and mars.json with 8). The game loads them at startup and places each artifact using its real latitude and longitude, measured from a reference point on each world (Apollo 11 on the Moon, Viking 1 on Mars). Terrain, gravity, sky and fog differ for Earth, the Moon and Mars. Every spacecraft model is built in code from basic shapes. The game works on desktop (keyboard and mouse) and mobile (on-screen joystick and touch).

Benefits and impact: Students and space fans learn the history of lunar and Mars missions by discovering the hardware themselves instead of reading a list. Because the quiz only covers what the player collected, it rewards actually reading the cards. It is free, needs no install, and runs in a browser.

Tools: HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, Three.js r128, the Web Audio API for sound effects (no audio files), JSON data files, and GitHub Pages for hosting.

Creativity: We turned the challenge from a report into a mission. The player's job is to collect and report facts, and passing depends on getting them right.

Factors considered: Cost: free and open to anyone. Energy and performance: a lightweight single-page build with low-poly models, a single instanced terrain mesh, and a limited play area, which we added after early lag. Accessibility: it works on phones and desktops with no install, but it does not yet support screen readers, and the info cards are text only. Improving this is future work.

Source code: https://github.com/marufkhanop/astro-web
